newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK'S Clarke denies threat to quit over EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK'S Clarke denies threat to quit over EMU.

text.p: Finance minister Kenneth Clarke denied on Thursday he had threatened to resign in a running row within the cabinet over Britain's attitude to the European Union's planned single currency.

Clarke issued the denial after a detailed account by BBC radio of the events leading up to a reaffirmation on Tuesday by Prime Minister John Major of the government's wait-and-see policy towards economic and monetary union (EMU).

The BBC report referred to fevered speculation that Clarke, the cabinet's leading pro-European, had threatened to quit if Major bowed to pressure from "Euro-sceptics" in his Conservative Party and ruled out signing up for EMU when it begins in 1999.

In the event, Major told parliament his position -- that he would keep his options open on membership -- had not changed and would not change before Britain's election, due by May 22. Major's statement was interpreted as a significant victory for Clarke and fellow pro-European Michael Heseltine, the deputy prime minister.
"I do not regard the BBC's account of this week's events as accurate. I did not threaten to resign and I am not threatening to resign," a Treasury statement issued on Clarke's behalf said.

Despite the denial, officials in the main opposition Labour Party sought to give credence to the BBC's account by telling reporters that Clarke was seen lunching on Wednesday at a swanky London restaurant with two BBC reporters.

The BBC said Clarke was furious with Conservative chairman Brian Mawhinney for letting aides spread the word that the ruling party would have a better chance of winning re-election if it came out explicitly against EMU.

Opinion polls show the Conservatives up to 20 percentage points behind Labour, which has been in opposition since 1979. However, Labour has adopted a virtually identical position on the single currency.
Divisions in Conservative ranks over Europe have dogged Major in his six years as prime minister and look set to stay in the headlines over the next 10 days.
Parliament will debate Europe for two days next Wednesday and Thursday and then Major will attend a weekend EU summit in Dublin at which plans for EMU will be at the top of the agenda.

Despite Major's explicit rejection of a policy shift before the election, Conservative Euro-sceptics opposed to closer European ties have made no secret of their determination to press the prime minister to at least sound a more dubious note.
The Dublin summit will also review plans to revise the EU's landmark 1991 Maastricht Treaty to prepare for the expansion of the 15-nation bloc to take in new members from eastern Europe.
Major told parliament he would have nothing to do with one expected feature of the draft revised treaty -- proposals for a common immigration policy and centralised border controls.
"There should be no doubt amongst any of our European partners that we are not prepared to accept any change whatever to the present system of safeguarding Britain's borders," he said.
